content: This report was made possible through the collaboration and contributions of various stakeholders. The development of this publication was supported by Cooperative Agreement Number GH001180 from the United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). The content of the report is solely the responsibility of the authors and does not necessarily represent the official views of the CDC. The objective of this report is to provide a detailed overview of the current status and trends in the global blood supply, including its safety, sufficiency, and usage. The report primarily relies on data from 2013, submitted by 156 of the 195 WHO Member States to the World Health Organization (WHO) Global Database on Blood Safety (GDBS). The GDBS was established in 1998 to collect data on the availability, safety, and accessibility of blood for transfusion. The main goal of the survey is to gather and analyze data on national blood systems to inform effective actions aimed at improving access to safe blood and blood products globally. Since 1998, the WHO Blood Transfusion Safety program has conducted biennial surveys on blood safety and availability in Member States. Starting in 2006, GDBS data has been collected annually using a standardized tool distributed to national health authorities or national blood transfusion services. For the years 2011, 2012, and 2013, web-based tools were employed for data collection. Standardized definitions of terms used in the survey questionnaire were developed to ensure consistency in reporting. Efforts were made to validate the data reported to WHO through regional and country offices, as well as through experts visiting countries on behalf of WHO. Discrepancies, inconsistencies, or unusual patterns in the data were clarified or corrected by contacting the respective countries. Additionally, GDBS data was compared with other published sources for validation, although systematic verification was not performed for all data provided by all countries. In 2013, 180 countries reported a total of 112.5 million blood donations, of which 9 million were apheresis donations. These donations were collected from various types of donors, including voluntary non-remunerated donors, family or replacement donors, and paid donors. The estimation of global blood collection took into account partial data provided by some countries. Annex 1 of the report provides details on the methodology used for this estimation. When analyzing blood donation and population data by WHO region and World Bank income group, significant variations in the availability of blood for transfusion were observed. For example, countries in the South-East Asia Region, which represent 26% of the global population, accounted for 15% of global blood donations. In contrast, the European Region, with only 11% of the global population, contributed 30% of global blood donations. Low-income and lower-middle-income countries, which together represent 48% of the global population, collected only 24% of global blood donations. In 2013, 78 of the 180 responding countries reported collecting blood through both whole blood donations and apheresis procedures. Of the total 112.5 million donations reported worldwide, 89% were whole blood donations, and 11% were apheresis donations. Apheresis donations were predominantly reported in the European Region, the Western Pacific Region, and the Region of the Americas, accounting for 20%, 15%, and 8% of total donations in these regions, respectively. Regarding the types of blood donors, 178 countries provided information on donations from voluntary non-remunerated donors, family/replacement donors, and paid donors. Seventy-four countries reported that more than 90% of their blood supply came from voluntary non-remunerated donors. However, 71 countries remained heavily reliant on family/replacement and paid donors, with these donations accounting for more than 50% of their blood supplies. In high-income countries, 95% of blood donations were from voluntary non-remunerated donors, compared to 79% in upper-middle-income countries, 71% in lower-middle-income countries, and 63% in low-income countries. The proportion of voluntary non-remunerated blood donations varied significantly across WHO regions, ranging from 51% in the Eastern Mediterranean Region to 97% in the Western Pacific Region. Between 2008 and 2013, 159 countries reported an increase of 10.7 million voluntary non-remunerated donations, with the highest percentage increases observed in the South-East Asia Region (75%) and the African Region (37%). Data on the sex profile of blood donors from 118 countries revealed that, overall, 30% of blood donations were given by female donors. However, there were substantial regional and country-level variations. For instance, in the Eastern Mediterranean Region, less than 10% of donations were from female donors in nine of the 12 reporting countries, while Egypt, Morocco, and Tunisia reported 54%, 40%, and 35% of donations from female donors, respectively. Age distribution data from 80 countries showed that globally, 40% of blood donations were from donors aged 25–44 years, 29% from donors aged 45–64 years, and 23% from donors aged 18–24 years. Only 5% of donations were from donors aged 65 years and older, and 3% were from donors younger than 18 years. In lowand middle-income countries, a higher proportion of donations came from younger donors compared to high-income countries, reflecting the age structure of populations in these regions. Demographic information about blood donors is crucial for developing and monitoring donor recruitment strategies to meet blood requirements. This includes addressing barriers to blood donation faced by specific populations. For example, in some developing countries, a relatively high donation rate was observed among individuals younger than 18 years, primarily school students. In contrast, in developed countries like France, Poland, and Singapore, the highest donation rates were reported among donors aged 18–24 years. However, in other developed countries such as Australia, the Netherlands, and New Zealand, older age groups had higher donation rates.
